title: Sensodyne's Parent Is Building a ₹2,000 Crore Factory in India. It Will Be the Company's Largest Plant Anywhere.
excerpt: Haleon, maker of Sensodyne, Centrum, and Crocin, will build its first Indian manufacturing site in Madhya Pradesh — a bet on India becoming the hub for its entire Asia supply chain.
body:
The company that makes Sensodyne, Centrum vitamins, and Crocin is placing its single largest manufacturing bet on India. Haleon, the consumer healthcare giant that spun out of GlaxoSmithKline in 2022, announced on Monday that it will invest £175 million — approximately $233.5 million or ₹2,000 crore — to build its first manufacturing plant in India, at Pithampur in Madhya Pradesh.

The investment is a departure for Haleon in India. Until now, the company has relied entirely on third-party contract manufacturers to produce its products for the Indian market. The new greenfield facility, expected to be operational by 2029-30, will focus on oral health products and create around 500 direct jobs.

"This will be our largest investment in India, where we see significant potential for the future," said Brian McNamara, Haleon's chief executive, at a media briefing. "We've probably done more rationalising the supply chain — shutting down plants rather than investing in creating a new manufacturing footprint. But now is the time. We're definitely in investment mode."

The reasoning is straightforward: India is now Haleon's second-largest oral care market globally, and Sensodyne is growing at a double-digit pace in the country. The oral health category in India is worth £1.8 billion, and Haleon commands a 71 per cent share of the therapeutic segment — the part of the market that sells on science-backed claims rather than whitening or freshness.

## Why India, Why Now

The timing aligns with a broader shift among global consumer companies toward in-country manufacturing in their fastest-growing markets. Reckitt, the maker of Mucinex and Dettol, has deepened its India supply chain. Unilever has long manufactured locally. What makes Haleon's move notable is the scale: ₹2,000 crore is a serious number for a company that has historically preferred asset-light models.

"While this facility will make our operations self-sufficient for India, we also expect it to become a key part of our global manufacturing network and export to key markets in the wider Asia region," said Kedar Lele, Haleon's India CEO and president of the Indian subcontinent business.

The choice of Pithampur, an established industrial hub near Indore in Madhya Pradesh, offers logistics advantages — centrally located in India, close to strong technical colleges, and well-connected by road and rail. The facility will also reduce Haleon's reliance on imported raw materials and finished products, insulating it from the kind of supply chain disruptions the West Asia crisis has intensified.

## The Make in India Angle

For India's manufacturing ambitions, the announcement is a small but meaningful data point. Foreign direct investment in manufacturing has been uneven, with most FDI flowing into services, technology, and financial sectors. Consumer healthcare — a category that directly touches hundreds of millions of households — represents the kind of labour-intensive, brand-driven manufacturing that the government's Make in India programme was designed to attract.

The investment follows Haleon's recent £65 million commitment to a new plant in Shanghai, China, as part of its strategy to reach one billion additional consumers globally by 2030. The company plans to expand distribution to over three million retail outlets in India, including deeper penetration into rural markets where oral health awareness is growing but access to premium products remains limited.

India's consumer health market is projected to exceed £23 billion by 2030, driven by rising incomes, growing health consciousness, and the structural shift toward preventive care. For the Indian diaspora, the Haleon bet is a reminder that the products their families use daily — Sensodyne, Eno, Iodex, Crocin — are increasingly being made for India, in India. This investment not only strengthens family ties back home but also enhances the availability of quality healthcare products for NRIs who wish to support their families with better health options. Furthermore, as India becomes a manufacturing hub, it could positively impact remittances and dual citizenship considerations for those looking to invest in their homeland.
